chapter: Early listening, piano and adolescent conflict
title: Methodist hymns versus Baptist rhythm: classes of black church music
summary: He explains how black church denominations differed in music, with Methodists cultured and Baptists known for clapping and chanting.

story.theme_name: Church, faith and religion in a musician's life
story.community_name: Church, faith and jazz: the sacred and the secular

blocks.x: So I think maybe these things had something to do with my getting away from the classical sounds as well as the environment that I lived in, particularly an all black congregation at the church where they were singing spiritual music, and I might add that this is a good point to talk about the types of music that I became interested in, which go into even the present day music of 1975. At that early age there was a classification of even black music, which was considered to be somewhat cultured and non-cultured.

And it was even divided, if I might say, into classifications of demonenations of churches. For instance as I said the Methodist church actually was not really totally accepted among black people because of the rigid cultured requirements.

Right. And at that time quite a number of blacks was associated with the Baptist church. And they were noted for more or less this rhythmic expression of what is now known as soul music, you know. But they were
known for their clapping and chanting, you know. Rather the /methodist church concentrated on the hymns, choir, hymns which was considered to be more cultured, if I might use the word, continually.
